calls.beyond: New Jersey has a better power play than most, and Vancouver has one of the league’s leakiest penalty kills. Even by those standards, this was a big night: New Jersey’s power play created 15.5 expected goals per 60, against their usual 8.2 (about 9.2 against Vancouver) and a league average of 7.6. A team strays this far about once every 20 games.

NJD.head: We gave New Jersey an 80% chance, and they delivered.

VAN.head: We gave Vancouver only a 20% chance, and it went the way we feared.

surprises.head: Both teams played to type
surprises.body: Nothing in this game strayed far from how these two usually play: the shot share, the quality of chances, special teams, hitting, ice time and goaltending all landed inside their normal night-to-night range.

story.head: The Devils take down the Canucks
paras: Amadeus Lombardi picked up his first NHL point. Linus Karlsson struck first for the Canucks on the power play early in the first, but they didn’t score again. Nico Hischier scored his 200th NHL goal on the power play less than three minutes later to tie it 1-1. Kevin Lankinen filled in for Leevi Meriläinen for 5:27 in the first before Vancouver went back to Meriläinen. Jesper Boqvist put the Devils ahead 2-1 late in the first, and Jesper Bratt made it 3-1 on the power play early in the second. Hischier scored his second of the night on the power play with just 10 seconds left in the period to make it 4-1. Hischier added an assist for a three-point night.

The Devils drove the play, outshooting the Canucks 37-21, and the scoreboard caught up. Jake Allen made 20 saves for the Devils. Nobody on the ice had a bigger night than Jack Hughes, by our Swing measure.
The Devils scored three power-play goals on four chances. The Devils improved to 2-2-0, and the Canucks dropped to 2-4-0.
